1.note: This line ends the gate's Hebrew subtitle ("In praise of an eloquent piece with a resh in every word, and the second to it"). "Utterly driven out" is Exod 11:1 (גָּרֵשׁ יְגָרֵשׁ), said there of Pharaoh sending Israel away.

2.he: דְּבַר אֵל יֵאָמַן / וטאעת אלרחמן / שְׁפַר עוֹבָדַיָּא
2.note: A poem in three languages. In each line the first part is Hebrew, the second Arabic (written in Hebrew letters, without vowels), and the third Aramaic. Ḥarizi names the three tongues below ("Aram, Eber, and Arabia"). The Arabic is rendered from the consonants; where the reading is doubtful there is a note.

3.note: Read as Arabic li-nuwwām al-balqaʿ, "for the sleepers of the barren land", that is, the dead in the earth. The reading is uncertain.

4.note: Read as Arabic sarā minhā sahmuhu, "its arrow went out from them". The referent (the poem? the words?) is not clear; the reading is uncertain.

5.note: Read as Arabic wa-yuhdīhā al-sharqu, "and the East sends it as a gift". Ḥarizi wrote the Taḥkemoni in the East after leaving Spain. Uncertain.

6.note: Literally "were pinched (or nipped) a pinching"; compare Job 33:6 קֹרַצְתִּי, "I was pinched off from clay", and Jer 46:20 קֶרֶץ. The English keeps the image; the sense is probably that they were struck with dread. Uncertain.

7.note: Literally "in something separate". It may mean a single, set-apart feat (the letter game that follows), or a composition on one theme. Uncertain.

8.note: The first composition: in the epistle and in the poem after it, every Hebrew word contains the letter resh (ר). The only exceptions are the frame words ("and he answered" here, and the lines that introduce the poem) and the word אֵל ("God") in the poem. The English does not imitate the constraint.

9.note: חֶרֶץ is rare; it is read here from Isa 10:22 כִּלָּיוֹן חָרוּץ, "destruction decreed". A meaning "cut, wound" (from חרץ, to cut) is also possible.

10.note: A pun on two senses of רְפָאִים: "shades" of the dead (Isa 26:14), whom his favor rouses, and the "giants" (Deut 2:11), whom his wrath slays.

11.he: יְרִימוּ צוּר וְיוֹצְרוֹ יִצְּרֵהוּ / בְּצָרָתוֹ כְּמִבְצָר מִמְּגוֹר צַר
11.note: The syntax of this line is unclear. "They exalt the Rock" (or "may they exalt") and "his Maker formed him" may be two clauses, or "the Rock and his Maker" one subject. The rendering is a guess.

12.note: The second composition: in the epistle and in the poem after it, no Hebrew word contains the letter resh. The exceptions are the frame word "and said" (וַיֹּאמַר), here and before the poem, and the word זִכְרוֹ ("his fame") in the line "The dead heard his fame and lived". The English does not imitate the constraint.

13.note: A pun: the name Ḥever (חֶבֶר) and מְחַבֵּר, "composer" (literally "one who joins together"). This is where the old man shows who he is.
